sentences.text: Wiehenvenator was a megalosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in northwestern Germany during the Middle Jurassic Callovian stage.
The type specimen consists of various bones from the Ornatenton Formation, including skull parts, jaw fragments, six teeth, tail vertebrae, ribs, a finger bone, leg bones, and ankle bones.

The fossil remains include parts of the skull, premaxilla, maxilla, a possible lacrimal bone, postorbital bones, the anterior part of a dentary, teeth, fused gastralia, two tail vertebrae, a complete rib, four rib fragments, an ilium, fibulae, and other elements.
Its maxilla is 82% the length of Torvosaurus gurneyi's maxilla, which is estimated at 10 meters, and its tail vertebrae and fibulae match those of Torvosaurus tanneri, estimated at 9 meters.
Mickey Mortimer estimated the skull length at nearly 1 meter and the total length at 7 to 8 meters with a weight of 0.75 to 1.2 tons.
The remains of Wiehenvenator were discovered in 1998 by geologist Friedrich Albat at the Pott quarry in the Wiehen Hills near Minden, Westphalia.
The discovery was initially known informally as the 'Minden Monster' due to extensive media attention and was also called Das Monster von Minden.
The species was formally named Wiehenvenator albati in 2016 by Rauhut, Hübner, and Lanser.
The specific name honors the discoverer, Friedrich Albat.
The fragmentary theropod skeleton was excavated between October 1998 and October 2001 alongside abundant marine invertebrates and fossilized wood.

Bone analysis suggests the individual was at least nine years old, possibly over ten, when it died, and histological analysis of fibulae indicates the known specimen was a large subadult approximately ten years old when it died.
Growth analysis indicates the specimen was a large subadult with slowing skeletal growth.
A report of a rib 50% larger than Allosaurus sparked speculation that the animal could reach 15 meters in length.
Thomas Holtz estimated the length of Wiehenvenator at 12 meters in 2012.
Other researchers concluded smaller dimensions, with Mickey Mortimer estimating a length of 7 to 8 meters and a weight of 0.75 to 1.2 metric tons.
Excavation teams returned to the site to search for additional material after the initial discovery.
Searching 35 meters around the formation yielded remains of the marine reptile Liopleurodon.
A second theropod was found 28.5 meters northwest of the original site in October 1999.
The crocodylomorph Metriorhynchus was discovered in an overgrown quarry in October 2014.

Wiehenvenator is classified within the Megalosauridae family as a sister taxon to Torvosaurus, and was classified in 2016 in the family Megalosauridae, specifically in the subfamily Megalosaurinae, as the sister taxon to Torvosaurus, its closest relative.
Wiehenvenator belongs to the superfamily Megalosauroidea.
The generic name combines a reference to Wiehengebirge, the German name for the Wiehen hills, with the Latin word venator, meaning 'hunter'.
Wiehenvenator lived during the Callovian stage, approximately 165.3 to 161.5 million years ago.
